# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is lazy. Left alone, it sits still, and when it does move, it only moves downhill. Everything about a municipal water system is an elaborate argument against this laziness—an engineered system of elevation, pressure, and power that convinces water to arrive at your kitchen sink on the 30th floor with enough force to rinse a plate. Understanding how this works requires only one physical idea, and then a lot of clever engineering built on top of it.

## The Fundamental Idea: Head

The single most important concept in water distribution is *hydraulic head*, which is just a fancy way of saying "the energy water has because of its elevation." Water at a height of 100 meters has 100 meters of head, and every 10 meters of elevation corresponds to roughly one atmosphere of pressure—about 14.7 pounds per square inch, or 100 kilopascals. This is why the classic municipal design is a water tower or hillside reservoir: if you store water 60 meters above the tallest building in town, gravity alone delivers about 6 atmospheres of pressure to every tap below it.
